days.title: Covert Tactics & Power Bases (*Reading the Move, Not Labeling the Person*)

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 1 — Covert Tactics & Power Bases (*Reading the Move, Not Labeling the Person*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** In `Bk4` you steered patterns across cooperative or stuck rooms; in `Bk5` you guard against covert pressure and power asymmetries—protecting your footing with cool clarity rather than paranoia or counter-aggression.

This expands your **White Belt W4 Starter Codex** into the full **6-Field Dark-Side Literacy Codex** (*context, range, harm, remedy, ethical use, your temptation*). Picture a table where the game shifts from open negotiation to covert pressure—guilt-tripping, selective inattention, shifting the goalposts, or using flattery right before a lopsided ask. Two rules keep your guard clean rather than paranoid. First, **read the tactic, not the type**: treat a single sharp or evasive move as possible style or stress (`Bk1`/`Bk2`), and treat repeated covert moves with built-in deniability as a pattern to answer directly without turning the other person into a caricature. Second, map the **bases of power** in play—formal/legitimate authority, specialized expertise, access to information, rewards, or coercive pressure—so you know whether you are negotiating terms or navigating structural leverage.
*Bridge to Tuesday:* Spotting the tactic and power base keeps you from swallowing the bait; tomorrow focuses on **declining the game openly** without fighting fire with fire.

cards.label: In Action
cards.title: Part 1 — Covert Tactics & Power Bases (*Reading the Move, Not Labeling the Person*)
cards.md:
- **Operational Bridge:** Name the specific behavior or tactic in plain language, anchor to the concrete issue or written record, and avoid taking on manufactured guilt.
- **Office Worked Example:** When a request is preceded by heavy flattery and followed by an unvetted scope push, thank them briefly for the kind words and respond strictly to the scope and timeline trade-off.
- **Personal Worked Example:** When someone shifts the goalposts or guilts you over a prior agreement, restate the specific commitment calmly without debating memory or apologizing for a boundary you already set.
- **Non-Example:** Diagnosing someone's character mid-conversation (*“You're being manipulative and playing the victim right now”*)—which escalates the fight rather than protecting your footing.
- **Decision Rule & Handoff:** Answer repeated covert tactics with calm, factual specificity and clear limits. Feeds your `Bk5` guarding strategy and walk-away discipline.

### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (French & Raven Power Bases + Written Trail)

When formal or coercive power is lopsided against you, verbal wit alone is insufficient; converting verbal understandings into neutral, confirming emails (*“To confirm what we agreed today…”*) shifts the power base from hidden memory to shared record.

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 2 — Declining the Game Openly (*Stepping Out Without Fighting Fire With Fire*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** Monday mapped covert tactics and power dynamics; **Tuesday** focuses on how to step out of a rigged or escalating game openly—without sinking into the exact combativeness or defensiveness you are declining.

Think of a coercive or zero-sum game as a trapdoor that only springs when you step onto the bait—either fighting fire with fire to win at any cost, or freezing in silent compliance. Declining the game openly means naming what is happening in calm, matter-of-fact terms, refusing the unhealthy game, and offering a clean alternative or boundary.
Holding a boundary under repeated pressure relies on staying anchored to observable actions rather than winning an ego contest—repeating a calm, steady boundary when needed, stating what *you* will do rather than demanding how they must feel, and keeping your tone grounded rather than reactive.
*Bridge to Wednesday:* Declining bad games cleanly protects everyday encounters; tomorrow draws the hard border between ordinary friction and **real danger**—where walk-away readiness and separation are the only sound moves.

### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (Dropping the Rope)

You cannot have a tug-of-war if one side sets the rope down. Dropping the rope calmly removes the counter-tension that keeps escalation alive—while leaving your boundary standing visibly in place.

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 3 — Real Danger, Walk-Away Readiness & Separation (*Staying Present Without Taking Yourself Hostage*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** Monday and Tuesday showed how to spot covert tactics and decline bad games openly; **Wednesday** closes `Bk5` by distinguishing **real danger** from mere discomfort—and keeping your willingness to walk away or separate intact.

Picture the difference between the ordinary friction of a hard negotiation and genuine harm or coercion. Stepping outside a frame should never mean floating into detached amusement while real stakes or boundaries are being crossed; at the same time, needing a deal or relationship at any cost takes *you* hostage.
A clear walk-away alternative (**BATNA**) and the option of physical or relational separation give boundaries real teeth. When a pattern is chronically coercive or harmful, stepping back, fencing off vulnerable topics, or walking away isn't failure—it is self-respect grounded in clarity.
*Bridge to Thursday & Friday:* You now hold all three `Bk5` pillars—tactic-over-type reading, open game exits, and walk-away discipline. Rehearse all five core tactics in Thursday's **Drop-the-Rope Lab** and lock in Friday's **Personal Tactic Codex**.

cards.label: In Action
cards.title: Part 3 — Real Danger, Walk-Away Readiness & Separation (*Staying Present Without Taking Yourself Hostage*)
cards.md:
- **Operational Bridge:** Separate ordinary discomfort from genuine harm or coercion, know your walk-away threshold ahead of time, and disengage or escalate formally when lines are repeatedly crossed.
- **Office Worked Example:** When a stakeholder repeatedly demands off-record compromises that violate policy or put you on the hook alone, state your boundary clearly, document the facts in writing, and walk away from unsafe terms.
- **Personal Worked Example:** When a dynamic consistently leaves you feeling small or pressured despite clear boundaries, step back to a safer distance rather than absorbing ongoing harm to keep the peace.
- **Non-Example:** Pretending everything is fine or staying in an unworkable deal out of fear of saying no.
- **Decision Rule & Handoff:** Never trade core dignity or safety to stay in a game; know your walk-away threshold before the pressure starts. Completes `Bk5` and sets up the final module, **`Bk6`**.

### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (Standing Rule 9 — Formal Channels)

When a room's psychological safety is low (`Bk1`) and covert coercion repeats (`Bk5`), informal relational repair is the wrong tool; switch cleanly to formal channels, written records, and external options.

:::note Resolved seam · Downshifting to Fit the Room vs. Diplomat Self-Erasure (`Bk2 Mon` vs. `Bk3 Mon` / `Bk5 Wed`)
**Tension.** `Bk2` directs you to *downshift* your proposal into a target room's native currency (speed, metrics, risk) and sequence, whereas `Bk3` demands a grounded bridge self and `Bk5` warns against compliance under pressure.

**Resolution.** **Translate the wrapper and sequence; never translate away the core stake.** Downshifting changes *how* and *when* your proposal enters the room, while your load-bearing boundary or requirement survives 100% intact. If the core ask vanishes in translation, you surrendered rather than brokered.
:::

cards.md:
## Deliberate Practice Lab — Five-Tactic Drop-the-Rope Rehearsal

:::note
Rehearse a calm, 1-to-2 sentence open exit aloud for each of these five covert tactics (in English and Spanish):
1. **Flattery → Lopsided Ask**
2. **Shifting the Goalposts**
3. **Manufactured Urgency / False Deadline**
4. **Guilt-Tripping / Score-Keeping**
5. **Off-Record Pressure Against Policy or Dignity**
:::

:::note
### 5-Tactic Drop-the-Rope Rehearsal Deck (Click to Reveal Exit)

:::details 1. Flattery → Lopsided AskTap to test exit
**Incoming Push:** “Honestly, you're the only person sharp enough to untangle this—can you absorb my Q3 audit tonight?”

**Calm Drop-the-Rope Exit:** “Thanks for saying that. I can't take on the Q3 audit tonight—let's look at priorities tomorrow at 10.”
:::

:::details 2. Shifting the GoalpostsTap to test exit
**Incoming Push:** “I know we said Tuesday, but leadership actually meant the full client deck, not just the draft.”

**Calm Drop-the-Rope Exit:** “Our Monday email locked the draft for Tuesday. If we're expanding to the full deck, delivery moves to Thursday—which do you prefer?”
:::

:::details 3. Manufactured UrgencyTap to test exit
**Incoming Push:** “If you don't sign off by 4 PM today, we'll have to move ahead without your team's input.”

**Calm Drop-the-Rope Exit:** “I notice we're being pushed to sign off before verifying the revised figures. I'll review tonight and confirm by 10 AM tomorrow.”
:::

:::details 4. Guilt-Tripping / Score-KeepingTap to test exit
**Incoming Push:** “After everything I covered for you last month, I thought you were a team player.”

**Calm Drop-the-Rope Exit:** “I appreciate your help last month, and I'm still not able to take on weekend scope this week.”
:::

:::details 5. Off-Record Pressure Against PolicyTap to test exit
**Incoming Push:** “Just between us, leave that exception off the summary so we don't spook the committee.”

**Calm Drop-the-Rope Exit:** “I'm not comfortable leaving a material exception off the record—I'll include it neutrally with our mitigation note, and follow up in writing.”
:::
:::
